features.name: Cache-first gathering, background sweep
features.description: The latency half of search-and-verify, and it is two functions rather than one because the guarantee belongs in the signature. resolve() runs at answer time and has no search parameter at all — not a default of None, not a flag — so there is no call site at which the network can be put on the critical path of a reply; the only thing that can fail is a dictionary lookup. sweep() runs in the background, is the only thing that reaches the network, and does so through an injected search function so the costing path never names a search backend. Same argument as FreshnessCache having no fetch method (AGT-012). A cached fact past its TTL SERVES with its staleness badge, because a labelled 40-day-old rate beats an error page; a fact never gathered is a Gap, because an old figure is probably right and says how old it is while an invented one is a coin flip that says nothing. A failed sweep does not evict a good cached fact — one bad fetch must not turn a working answer into a gap — and a marketplace listing never overwrites a Tier-1 or Tier-2 fact, which would silently demote a costable line to context.
acceptance_criteria: resolve() has no search or fetch parameter — asserted by an introspection test
A key with no cached fact produces a named Gap, never an estimate
A stale cached fact is served and flagged, not withheld
A cached Tier-3 fact is returned as context AND as a gap, never as a costable fact
The sweep skips keys not yet due for refresh; force re-reads regardless of age
A failed admission leaves the previously cached fact in place
A CONTEXT_ONLY result never overwrites a costable cached fact
A model-authored search result never reaches the cache
features.risk: P0. Without the signature split, opening search to the agents puts six portals on the critical path of every reply, and the first deadline turns 'check the cache' into 'just fetch it here'.

features.name: Deterministic page extractors
features.description: The half of search-and-verify that decides whether the idea works: the thing that actually reads a figure off a page. Four refusals. The extractor NAMES ITSELF — extracted_by is set inside these functions and is never a parameter, so a caller cannot label a model's guess 'html_table_cell' and walk it past a gate that only compares strings. Cells are located by row and column HEADERS, never by index, because rows[3][2] keeps parsing cleanly after someone inserts a column and silently returns a different number with no error anywhere. Ambiguity is refused rather than resolved: a label appearing twice with two different figures returns nothing, since taking the first is a guess wearing a deterministic costume and arrives with a provenance trail attesting a parser did it. And the raw page text is preserved as raw_value — '5 per cent', '₹1,50,000' — so admission re-parses in the open and a human auditing the fact sees what the page said rather than what a parser concluded. An empty cell is not a zero. HTML parsing is on the standard library, not BeautifulSoup, which is undeclared in requirements.txt and would work in development and fail in a clean install.
acceptance_criteria: No extractor accepts extracted_by as a parameter — asserted by introspection
Every extractor label appears in extractors.deterministic in admission.yaml
A label with two different figures beside it yields nothing, with the conflict named
Table cells resolve by header; an inserted column does not shift the answer
An empty cell is refused rather than read as zero
A vague column header matching several columns is refused
lakh and crore scale words are applied; the same figure written two ways is not a conflict
Repeated extraction over the same bytes yields the same figure
No agents/, tools/ or orchestrator/ module constructs a CandidateFact by hand — AST ratchet
features.risk: P0. Everything upstream can be correct and still worthless if the thing reading the page is a model with a regex bolted on for appearances. This is where that is prevented or not.

features.name: Landed cost model
features.description: Three figures kept distinct, because most tooling conflates them: ex-showroom, on-road (plus GST, road tax, registration, insurance) and LANDED (minus subsidies, minus input tax credit, minus the income-tax effect of depreciation). GST is resolved against the schedule in force ON THE PURCHASE DATE, since GST 2.0 restructured everything mid-year on 22 September 2025. ITC on a passenger vehicle is BLOCKED under s.17(5) unless the use is resale, passenger transport, driving instruction or goods transport — a GST-registered consultancy buying a car gets nothing, and the reason is stated rather than the line silently omitted. Depreciation applies the half-rate rule under 180 days of use. See docs/PROCUREMENT_SCOPE.md. COVERAGE (2026-08-13): the four-state road tax table was a ceiling on the product, not a floor. A rate admitted through the gather layer now takes precedence over the pack, so a state arrives by being SOURCED rather than by being typed into this repository; the pack remains the verified baseline for the states it covers and the raise remains for a state with neither. Nothing is averaged at any point. A gathered fact wins over the pack deliberately — it is dated, carries its URL, and was re-read more recently than the file, which is a hand-taken snapshot of the same thing.
acceptance_criteria: GST 2.0 structure correct (0/5/18/40); 12% and 28% removed
EV GST at 5%
Road tax for any state via an admitted fact, the verified pack, or an explicit raise — never an average
A gathered fact takes precedence over the pack entry
The EV-specific key is preferred for an electric vehicle
ITC only when GST-registered and business use; blocked under s.17(5) with the reason stated
Depreciation half-rate rule when used under 180 days
Stamp duty comes from the gather layer, not a table (see PRC-007)
features.risk: HELD AT `tested`, NOT `verified`. Two acceptance criteria are unmet and one data set is deliberately partial. (1) ROAD TAX COVERAGE IS FOUR STATES (KA, MH, DL, TN) out of thirty-odd. An unlisted state RAISES rather than averaging, because an averaged road tax is wrong by tens of thousands while looking authoritative — but that means most users are not yet servable and the registry should say so. (2) Customs duty and compensation cess are not modelled. (3) The state figures are indicative and need re-verification against each state transport department before they drive a user-facing cost; the PRC-002 tier system is what will carry that. The blocked-ITC rule, the GST effective-dating and the 180-day depreciation boundary are all mutation-tested.

features.name: Purchase eligibility and subsidy engine
features.description: Date-windowed evaluation of what a purchase benefit is WORTH, not only whether it is available. CORE-009 carried a scalar max_benefit, which forced four different shapes into one: a flat deduction ceiling, a per-kWh incentive with a cap, a percentage of benchmark cost, and a capacity slab. Finding the bug that caused: PM E-DRIVE carried benefit_per_kwh: 2500 beside max_benefit: 5000 and the evaluator read only the second, so every two-wheeler was quoted 5,000 including a 1.5 kWh model actually worth 3,750. A fifth kind, UNVERIFIED, reports a scheme that demonstrably exists but whose amount has not been confirmed against a Tier-1 source — because writing down a secondary site's number is what the admission gate refuses from a search result and the rule pack gets no exemption from its own rule, and recording zero reads as 'worth nothing to you', a false statement dressed as a computed one. Entitlement and quantum are kept as separate questions: a missing amount input leaves status ELIGIBLE and surfaces through amount_missing_fields, because collapsing it into INSUFFICIENT_DATA would say 'we cannot tell whether you qualify', which is false. total_claimable returns the sum AND everything it could not include. Buyer profile is a condition dimension with a closed vocabulary, ratcheted by test: a typo'd profile never matches and never errors, so the rule would be silently dead for every user forever. See docs/PROCUREMENT_SCOPE.md.

PM E-DRIVE correctly excludes electric cars
e-2W/e-3W incentive computed at 2,500 per kWh and capped at 5,000, with the cap as a traced step
PM-Surya Ghar CFA is a MARGINAL TIERED rate, matching the ministry's own worked examples at 1.5 kW, 2.5 kW and 6 kW

total_claimable returns the unquantified outcomes alongside the total
Every buyer_profile used in a rule is in meta.buyer_profiles
A malformed benefit block raises rather than degrading to zero

features.name: Dated signal ledger (timing)
features.description: NOT a price forecast, and built so it cannot quietly become one. A Signal carries no field for a predicted price, probability or direction — there is nowhere to put one — and every sentence is rendered from a per-kind template, so there is no code path where a claim about what a price will do could be composed. Four kinds: POLICY_CLIFF (a scheme window, taken from the eligibility engine rather than a second list of dates, so the product has one source of truth about when 80EEB shut), RATE_CHANGE (GST effective dates, described as out of date rather than as a different opinion), TAX_BOUNDARY (31 March), and OBSERVED_PATTERN, whose rupee impact is None BY TYPE — the constructor raises if one is attached, because 'this happened in 2021-24' plus a figure is a forecast wearing a fact's clothes, and it raises again if the years observed are missing, because without them it reads as a general truth about the market. The 31 March boundary is the only timing effect here that is arithmetic rather than judgement, and it is stated as a DEFERRAL: the half not claimed now returns through the written-down value, so the figure is tax brought forward by a year, not money saved. It is computed under the current pack alone — running the 1 April side would need next year's rules, and standing in the current pack for them would break the no-default-financial-year rule from the inside.
acceptance_criteria: Every dated signal has a date, a source and a rupee impact where computable
No output predicts a price movement — asserted by regex over every sentence the module can produce
An observed pattern cannot carry a rupee impact; the constructor raises
An observed pattern must state the years observed; the constructor raises
A pattern can never reach the quantified total, by construction
The 31 March effect is computed through the costing model and described as a deferral, not a saving
No boundary signal for a buyer with no depreciation
No scheme date is hardcoded in this module — asserted over the AST
features.risk: P1 integrity. A product that implies it can predict gold or property prices does harm.

features.name: Dealer quote teardown
features.description: A quotation for anything — dealer, vendor, contractor, builder — torn down line by line against an already-computed landed cost, so this module cannot drift from the cost model. Padding hides in the NAMING: a line called 'handling' is negotiable, a line called 'RTO' is not, and a quote calling a handling fee 'RTO charges' relies on the buyer not knowing the difference. Matching is longest-term-first on a normalised label, because 'RTO Registration Charges' contains both terms and they compare against completely different figures. TWO TOTALS, never one: `overcharged` is where a statutory figure is wrong and is arguable in writing; `negotiable` is charges with no statutory basis, which are legal. Adding them hands a buyer a single number, part of which they will be told — correctly — that they agreed to, and the argument then collapses and takes the defensible half with it. Deltas never go negative, so an under-charged line cannot net off a real overcharge. Flags GST at the abolished 12% and 28% slabs, still quoted by dealer software that has not been updated and the largest single error available. TCS under s.206C(1F) is reported as NOT A COST — it is the buyer's own tax collected early, creditable and visible in Form 26AS — and is checked at 1% of the ENTIRE consideration above 10 lakh, not of the excess. A line the engine cannot price is reported as UNCHECKED, never omitted, because 'three issues found' reads as 'everything else is fine'. No output has any opinion on whether a price is high.
acceptance_criteria: Line items extracted and mapped to model components by longest matching term
Discrepancy report with rupee deltas; deltas never negative
GST at an abolished slab (12%, 28%) flagged with the abolition date
An EV quoted at the petrol rate is caught
Charges with no statutory basis are reported as negotiable, never as an overcharge
The two totals are reported separately and never summed
TCS reported as recoverable, checked on the entire consideration, and refused below the threshold
Unrecognised lines reported as UNCHECKED with a coverage statement
A quote whose lines do not sum to its stated total is flagged first
No finding calls a price high, expensive or a bad deal
features.risk: Highest practical value in Phase 6: it works on the user's real price, and dealer quotations are where padding hides.

features.name: Property purchase pack
features.description: The circle-rate trap, computed as TWO provisions rather than one warning. Where the deed price is below the stamp duty value, s.50C deems the stamp duty value to be the seller's consideration for capital gains — tax on money that never reached them — and s.56(2)(x) charges the buyer with the whole excess as income from other sources — tax on a gift they did not receive. The tolerances are NOT symmetric: 50C is a flat 10%, 56(2)(x) is 50,000 or 10% whichever is HIGHER, so on a 4,00,000 plot a 45,000 shortfall taxes the seller and not the buyer. A single combined warning is wrong for one of its two readers. Verifying the safe harbour is itself a trap worth recording: the department's own s.50C page is a 2018 snapshot carrying 105%, and the Finance Act 2020 raised it to 110% — reading the section page alone, the obvious diligent thing to do, encodes a tolerance half the true size. Stamp duty is deliberately NOT a table here; thirty-odd states with women-buyer and urban variants revised at every state Budget is what road tax already showed the cost of, so a rate arrives through the gather layer as an admitted fact or the line is a named Gap. A woman buyer with no concessional rate held is told the figure may be higher than she will pay, rather than silently charged the general rate. RERA is surfaced, never claimed as checked.
acceptance_criteria: Seller (50C) and buyer (56(2)(x)) exposures are computed separately with their own tolerances
The 50,000 floor makes the two limbs diverge on a small transaction — tested
The tolerance is 10%, not the 5% on the department's 2018 section snapshot
A price above the circle rate is not a shortfall
An ungathered state raises rather than averaging; the pack reports a named gap
The women-buyer rate is preferred where held, and its absence is stated
RERA absence is flagged as a question, and a recorded number is not claimed to be verified
No output expresses a view on the locality, the timing or the price
features.risk: Regulatory restraint required. Compute costs; do not forecast markets.

features.name: Rewrite price_intelligence agent
features.description: Mostly a deletion. The agent carried a hardcoded Cost Inflation Index table ending at FY 2024-25 that fell back to 254 or 363 for anything newer, so a FY 2025-26 acquisition indexed silently against 2015-16; the official table (Notification 70/2025, including 2025-26 = 376 and 2026-27 = 384) now lives in the rule pack, where an unknown year RAISES. It also carried a post-tax yield comparison across FDs, ELSS, gold, SGBs and debt funds in which every number was invented — FD 7.5%, ELSS 12%, gold 6%, all hardcoded floats shown as though computed — applied a 10% LTCG rate that has been 12.5% since 23 July 2024, ignored the 1.25 lakh exemption while naming it, and recommended buying Sovereign Gold Bonds whose primary issuance stopped in February 2024. The rates could have been corrected; that was not the problem. Ranking investment products by projected return for a named individual IS personalised investment advice, SEBI-regulated and outside scope, so the branch was deleted rather than fixed and the agent says why, plus what it can do instead. What remains is indexation routed through the tool layer to the core engine — indexation survives as an ELECTION for a resident individual or HUF selling immovable property acquired before 23 July 2024, and will for decades. The agent now does no arithmetic at all and moved from the AGT-001 legacy budget (8 sites) into THIN_AGENTS.

No invented yield figure remains — asserted by AST over float constants
No financial-year-keyed table remains in the agent

features.name: SmartSavings and PurchaseAdvisor rebuild
features.description: Comparison across purchase options, ranked by LANDED COST rather than sticker price — which is where options actually differ, since an EV and a petrol car at the same ex-showroom price are lakhs apart on the road. Three things are kept structurally apart: computed cost lines, each rendered through the Money component so a figure with no provenance cannot appear at all; observed marketplace listings, badged unverified with the date seen, in their own section, never added to anything; and gaps, named with what would fix them, because a breakdown that silently drops the road tax for an uncovered state looks identical to one where it is genuinely nil. THE COMPONENT DOES NO ARITHMETIC — every total displayed comes from the backend, so there is no code path by which a listing could reach one, and a test proves it by rendering with and without a listing. Closed windows are shown rather than filtered: knowing a window shut, and when, is more useful than an empty list. Signals render the ledger's own sentences, so the component cannot compose a forecast. Ordering uses a decimal sort key the backend supplies rather than parsing a rupee display string, and an unusable key leaves the order stable rather than confidently wrong.

Gaps rendered with what would fix them

features.name: Composed confidence model

Signals: (1) input provenance, official-document > parsed > user-stated > system-assumed; (2) rule freshness from last_verified; (3) input completeness, which required fields are present; (4) assumption count, how many defaults were substituted; (5) source tier for procurement facts. Emits a BREAKDOWN, not an opaque number.

features.name: Reproducibility and integrity
features.description: Each pack pins the rule-pack VERSION — the year plus a SHA-256 of the pack file's bytes, added as TaxRuleset.content_hash — rather than its self-declared verified_on date, because a date is a claim inside the file and a hash is a fact about it. Pinning the date lets someone change a rate without bumping it and have the pack replay clean. Three questions are kept separate: is the pack intact (content hash), does it replay under the same pinned pack, and is it still right today (recompute under the CURRENT pack and diff). The diff refuses to collapse the two answers — it shows the figures as issued and as they stand now, with both rule-pack versions, behind a headline the reader sees before any number.

features.name: DPDP Act 2023 compliance
features.description: Handling income figures and PAN makes this a Data Fiduciary under the DPDP Act 2023; v1's README claimed compliance with nothing behind it, which is worse than claiming nothing because it is a representation to users. Four structural decisions. Consent is PER PURPOSE and against a NOTICE VERSION: one `consent: true` column cannot express s.6, and a consent recorded against notice v1 does not carry to v3 if the wording for that purpose changed — the person was informed of something else. A version bump that reworded an UNRELATED purpose does not invalidate this one, because invalidating everything on every edit trains people to click through. Withdrawal is the same shape as granting — `withdraw()` takes the same arguments as `grant()`, asserted by a signature test, because s.6(6) is a property of the interface not a promise in a policy document. Retention is a JOB, not a paragraph: `due_for_erasure` returns exactly what a scheduled run must delete today, and a withdrawal makes data due immediately rather than at the end of its window. And erasure is VERIFIED PER STORE: a delete that reports success without confirming produces a compliance record asserting something untrue, so a store with no confirmer is a failure — 'we have no way to check' is not 'it is gone'. The consent record survives withdrawal, because deleting it destroys the evidence consent was ever held.

Erasure verified per store; an unconfirmable delete is a failure
Controls mapped to obligations in docs/dpdp_controls.md, with gaps named

features.name: Auth hardening
features.description: Three holes, and the third made the other two matter. A token carried nothing identifying it, so there was no handle to revoke — every issued token now carries jti and family, defaulting to fresh ids so a caller that forgets still produces a revocable token rather than an anonymous one that escapes every check. get_current_user never looked at the sessions table: a row was written at login and read by nothing, so logging out deleted a record while the token in an attacker's hands kept working for the rest of its fifteen minutes. And a refresh token was reusable for a week. Rotation now makes a refresh token SINGLE USE, and a second presentation revokes THE WHOLE FAMILY: two parties hold that token and there is no way to tell which is presenting it, so both must re-authenticate. That does log the real user out; the alternative is guessing which of two identical requests is the thief, and guessing wrong leaves the thief with a valid session. There is deliberately NO GRACE WINDOW for double-submits — that window is a replay window. All rejection causes raise one exception type, because a different status or message per cause is an oracle telling an attacker whether a token was ever real and whether they have been detected. A token with no family is REJECTED rather than waved through: tokens minted before rotation existed have none, and treating 'no family' as 'not revoked' would keep exactly the tokens this exists to stop. Timestamps are timezone-aware throughout — datetime.utcnow() returns a naive value that claims to be UTC. The store is injected behind a protocol, with InMemorySessions as the reference implementation the semantics are defined by.
acceptance_criteria: Every issued token carries jti and family
A refresh token is single use; the successor stays in the same family
Reuse revokes the entire family, including the legitimate successor
No grace window — reuse at the same instant is still reuse
An unknown jti revokes nothing (a forged token must not be a denial of service)
A revoked family stops an access token immediately, not at expiry
A token with no family claim is rejected
Logout ends the family, not just the presented token
All causes raise one exception type — no oracle for the client
No naive utcnow() in the token path

VERIFIED LIVE (2026-08-17): full register -> refresh -> reuse-detection -> family-revocation -> get_current_user-rejects cycle exercised via real HTTP requests against a running app with a live Postgres (docker-compose). Found and fixed a real bug in the process: sessions.expires_at was a naive DateTime column while every caller builds an aware datetime, crashing the first real registration attempt with a 500 (backend/db/orm_models.py, migration prd_002_sessions_tz_aware).
features.risk: P0 security.

features.name: Rate limiting and abuse controls
features.description: Three problems usually lumped together that want OPPOSITE answers when things break. Rate limiting fails OPEN: taking the service down because the limiter is down converts a degradation into an outage and does the attacker's job. Spend caps fail CLOSED: an unavailable counter means we do not know what has been spent today, and 'unknown' is not a number you can be under — a store outage must not become an unbounded bill. Getting those backwards is the classic mistake. Limits are a TOKEN BUCKET, not a fixed window: 60/minute as a window lets a caller send 60 at 11:59:59 and 60 more at 12:00:00, which is exactly the burst the limit was written to prevent; a bucket crossing the same boundary grants one more, not another sixty. Per-user and per-IP are both applied, because a user limit alone is evaded by making accounts and an IP limit alone is evaded from a phone. The LLM cap RESERVES an estimate before the call and reconciles the true cost after — checking the bill afterwards is checking whether the money is already gone, and an underestimate then overshoots by at most one call rather than by a runaway loop. Uploads are typed by MAGIC BYTES, never by extension or declared type: a file named invoice.pdf starting with PK is a zip, and check_upload returns the SNIFFED type so a caller cannot accidentally trust the uploader's word. Size is refused DURING the read, because reading a 4 GB upload into memory to discover it is too large is the attack.
acceptance_criteria: Token bucket, not a fixed window — the boundary grants the rate, not the capacity
The bucket never refills past capacity
The reported retry-after is actually long enough
Per-user and per-IP limits both applied; a missing key does not bucket everyone together
The LLM estimate is reserved before the call and reconciled after
The spend cap fails CLOSED; the rate limiter fails OPEN
The cap is per user and resets daily
Uploads typed by magic bytes; a renamed zip, a real PNG and a declared/actual mismatch are all refused
Oversized uploads refused during the read, not after
No refusal echoes the uploaded bytes back

VERIFIED LIVE (2026-08-17): RateLimitMiddleware exercised against the running app — 429s with a correct Retry-After at exactly the configured capacity. Redis-backed RedisLimiter (backend/middleware/redis_ratelimit.py) built and verified against a live Redis, including a concurrent-requests test proving the Lua script's atomicity (no double-grant of the last token); the middleware prefers Redis and falls back to per-process on connection failure. Upload validation (magic bytes, streamed size cap) wired into backend/api/knowledge.py.
features.risk: P0 abuse and cost control. An uncapped LLM endpoint behind auth is still a spend vector.

features.name: Observability
features.description: Two halves. The PII-redacting log formatter is the half that is a correctness problem rather than a plumbing one: nobody types logger.info(pan) — PII reaches logs incidentally, through an exception whose message quotes the row it failed on or a dict dumped for debugging. So redaction is applied at the FORMATTER, the single point every line passes through, rather than at call sites, which is a rule someone has to remember. Redaction is BY SHAPE, not by field name: an allowlist misses `pan_of_spouse`, `payload["PAN"]` and an identifier mid-sentence. Aadhaar is the interesting case — twelve digits alone would redact rupee amounts and timestamps, making the logs useless and training people to disable the filter, so the Verhoeff checksum every Aadhaar carries is what separates a real one from a coincidence. Composes with PRD-005's secret redaction rather than reimplementing it. The second half is metrics, and the same argument decides what to measure: request rate, error rate and latency would not have caught a single defect this project has found. A service can serve every request in 200ms with a 200 status and be telling people the wrong tax. So the metrics that lead are the ones watching the safety properties — answers served vs amended vs WITHHELD, and reviewer findings by verdict and category. A rising withheld rate means the analyst has started producing answers the reviewer will not stand behind, and a withheld rate that falls to zero means either the model improved or the reviewer stopped working, which are worth being able to tell apart. What it does NOT do is make logs publishable: free text a user typed is still personal data, and the answer to that is not logging free text.
acceptance_criteria: PAN, GSTIN, email and Indian phone numbers redacted wherever they appear
Aadhaar redacted only on a valid Verhoeff checksum; other 12-digit numbers survive
An exception traceback is redacted — the line nobody wrote
install() wraps existing handlers rather than adding or replacing one
Ordinary log lines are unchanged
setup_logging installs the redacting formatter over every handler, asserted end to end

finsage_answers_total{outcome} distinguishes served / amended / withheld, recorded inside pipeline.run rather than at call sites — the same argument as redacting at the formatter, because a caller that forgets is a metric that undercounts silently

Label cardinality is ENFORCED, not documented: `_LABEL_VALUES` declares the permitted values and a sample outside them is dropped and counted rather than recorded. An unbounded label is a memory leak that looks healthy in testing and takes the process down weeks later, which is too easy to introduce by accident to leave to convention. A test asserts every label in use is either declared or on a named exception list.
HTTP metrics label by ROUTE TEMPLATE (/api/v1/users/{user_id}), never the resolved path; every unmatched path collapses to one series so a scanner probing random URLs cannot inflate the metrics store

/metrics requires a bearer token in production and returns 404 — not 401 — without one, so an unauthenticated caller learns nothing about whether it exists. Open in development, because a token on a local Prometheus is friction people route around.

Recording never breaks a request: every recorder swallows its own exceptions, logs the first of each kind, and counts the rest in finsage_metrics_errors_total so a permanently broken recorder is visible
Scrapes are not counted as traffic — otherwise an idle service shows a request rate set by the scrape interval
build_info carries the rule-pack version, so a change in the withheld rate can be correlated with a change in the law underneath it

VERIFIED by mutation (2026-08-23): disabling the cardinality guard fails 2 tests; labelling by resolved path fails 2; removing the token check fails 1; letting a recorder raise fails 1; counting the scrape fails 1; deleting the record_pipeline_result call from the pipeline fails all 4 wiring tests.

STILL OPEN: OpenTelemetry traces, Sentry, and a dashboard definition. Metrics answer 'is it happening'; traces answer 'where did the 8 seconds go', which is DEM-005's question and needs the p95 measurement first.
features.risk: Medium. The metrics layer cannot break a request by construction and is tested for it. The residual risk is operational rather than functional: under gunicorn with several workers each worker keeps its own registry, so counters appear to move backwards unless PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR is set to a writable, empty directory that is cleared on restart. That requirement is stated by `multiprocess_mode_note()` in code rather than only in a runbook, so the two cannot drift apart — but nothing enforces it, and a multi-worker deployment that misses it will produce confusing graphs rather than an error.

features.name: Secrets management
features.description: config.py shipped auth.secret_key defaulting to 'your-super-secret-key-change-in-production'. Any deployment that never set the variable signed its JWTs with a constant in a public repository — the app started, every test passed, and the only symptom was that authentication worked for everybody. Two decisions close it. FAIL AT STARTUP, not at first login: an app that boots and then 500s on /auth/login looks like a bug in the login endpoint, while one that refuses to boot naming the variable is diagnosed in ten seconds. And THERE IS NO SHARED DEFAULT ANY MORE: in development the key is a fresh random value per process, so there is no published constant to leak and none to accidentally deploy — a dev login no longer survives a restart, which is a small price and arguably correct. Production has no default at all. The audit catches placeholder shapes, secrets too short to resist offline brute force against an HS256 signature, and length without variety (a 64-character run of one letter is a one-character secret). It reports EVERY problem rather than the first, so an operator does not learn about debug mode on the deployment after the one that fixed the key. Development logs and continues, because a checker that blocks local work gets disabled and then is not checking production either. Nothing ever prints a secret: messages name the setting, redact() strips every configured value from a log line plus credentials inside any URL by shape, and fingerprint() is comparable but not reversible.
acceptance_criteria: No secret constant in the repository — asserted against config.py by test
The app refuses to start in production on a placeholder, short or low-variety secret
The development default is random per process
Every problem is reported at once, not just the first
Development warns and continues rather than blocking
No message, error or log line ever contains the secret itself
redact() strips configured secrets and URL credentials it has never seen
Loopback origins are not flagged; a plaintext public origin is
features.risk: P0. config.py currently defaults to 'your-super-secret-key-change-in-production'.

Restore procedure documented with an assertion step, not just a restore step
Zero-downtime migration approach documented

features.name: Load and resilience testing

features.name: Analyst agent (CA standard)
features.description: First pass. Understands the question, gathers facts, calls deterministic tools, drafts an explanation to the standard a chartered accountant would apply advising a client. Computes NOTHING: every figure comes from backend/core.
acceptance_criteria: No arithmetic on money anywhere in the agent or its prompts
No prompt asks the model for a rupee amount
Every claim maps to a tool result it actually received
States what it could not determine rather than filling the gap
features.risk: The generator half of the pipeline. Its failure mode is omission, which is exactly what AGT-009 exists to catch.

features.name: Reviewer agent — CA file-review pass
features.description: Adversarial second pass with FULL independent engine access. Checks what the Analyst said and, more importantly, what it did not: omitted regime comparisons, dropped closed windows, misleading framing over correct numbers, unasked questions that would change the answer. Because it can call the engine itself, every challenge it raises is deterministically proven rather than one model's opinion against another's.
acceptance_criteria: Can independently call the tax engine, eligibility engine and rule packs
Every challenge cites the engine call that substantiates it
CANNOT edit or override any figure — a disagreement is a bug report against the engine, never a silent correction
Catches a seeded omission (better regime not mentioned) in the eval corpus
Catches a seeded closed-window drop
features.risk: Two LLMs marking each other's homework produces CORRELATED error. This is only safe because the reviewer's authority is the deterministic engine, not its own judgement about numbers.

features.name: Reviewer agent — assessment risk pass
features.description: Conditional third pass in the voice of an Assessing Officer: what would draw a query, what looks aggressive, where is documentation thin. Runs only when the output actually contains a claim, deduction or recommendation — a purely informational answer skips it, which is what keeps p95 tolerable.
acceptance_criteria: Skipped for informational answers; triggered by any claim or recommendation
Flags thin documentation without suppressing a legitimate entitlement
Over-caution is itself a tracked failure: eval asserts it does not FLAG a fully documented standard claim
features.risk: An AO-voiced reviewer drifts toward suppressing valid claims. The false-alarm eval is the counterweight and must stay green.

features.name: Graded review verdicts (block / amend / flag)
features.description: BLOCK withholds the answer and forces one redraft, then fails visibly rather than degrading to the unreviewed draft. AMEND appends the missing caveat verbatim. FLAG shows the answer with a visible note. No verdict may silently rewrite content, so the user always sees what was contested.
acceptance_criteria: Exactly one redraft on BLOCK; a second BLOCK surfaces an explicit failure, never the unreviewed draft
AMEND text appears verbatim; the Analyst cannot paraphrase it away
Review findings are recorded in the Evidence Pack, including ones that were resolved
No code path lets a review verdict alter a figure
features.risk: Silent rewriting would hide disagreement from the user, which defeats the purpose of having a reviewer at all.

features.name: Answer-time source freshness check
features.description: Answer time reads a cache and never the network — the cache has no fetch method at all, and a test asserts that, because a cache that COULD fetch would eventually be asked to. Four states: FRESH, STALE, CHANGED and UNKNOWN, where silence never reads as confirmation. A verdict never blocks an answer; it downgrades confidence and shows a badge, with a changed source costing most (0.25) because it is the only state where the underlying fact may be WRONG rather than merely unconfirmed. Filled by a background sweep whose failure can only age facts into STALE.
acceptance_criteria: Cache hit adds under 50ms
A network failure never blocks an answer — it downgrades confidence and shows a staleness badge
A detected upstream change flags the affected rule and notifies rather than silently recomputing
features.risk: Low. The sub-50ms criterion is measured over 1,000 lookups so a single fast call cannot pass by luck; a dictionary lookup comes in far under it. Network failure cannot block an answer because there is no network call on the path — that is the design, not a resilience feature.
